claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at% Al to a Mo-Nb-Ta-W-based refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can produce a uniform distribution of the added Al.
The proposed improvement should occur during exposure at approximately 1200°C in 1 atm O2 for up to 100 hours.
The Al-modified alloy will form a continuous, dense Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature oxygen exposure.
Al selectively oxidizes at the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
Selective oxidation of Al generates an impermeable Al2O3 layer.
The Al2O3 layer suppresses oxygen penetration into the substrate.
Suppression of oxygen penetration minimizes substrate degradation and slows oxidation kinetics.
The Al-doped alloy will exhibit significantly lower oxidation-induced mass gain than the undoped alloy.
The Al-doped alloy will develop a thinner oxide scale than the undoped alloy.
The mass gain and oxide-scale thickness may be reduced by more than half relative to the undoped baseline.
An equivalent alloy with negligible Al will experience more severe oxidation damage under the same conditions.
The alloy with negligible Al will exhibit more oxide-scale spalling and higher mass gain than the Al-modified alloy.
Performance may degrade when Al content exceeds approximately 10 at%.
Al contents above approximately 10 at% may promote brittle-phase formation.
Inadequate homogenization may produce inhomogeneous oxide scales and degrade oxidation performance.
The optimal Al addition and associated mechanical-property trade-offs remain to be established experimentally.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-cast alloy, but the experiment subjects both the Al-free and Al-containing samples to homogenization. The tested control therefore does not clearly match the defined baseline state.
The hypothesis describes homogenizing the alloy 'by arc melting,' whereas the intervention distinguishes arc melting from a subsequent homogenization heat treatment.
